title: House Passes $95 Billion Budget Framework for Iran War and Election Overhaul
excerpt: The budget resolution cleared the House 216-214, funding defense spending for the Middle East conflict and Trump's SAVE America Act, but faces an uncertain path in the Senate.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • House passed a $95 billion budget framework with a narrow 216-214 vote.
  • Allocations include $60 billion for defense and $10 billion for election reforms.
  • Trump's SAVE America Act aims for voter ID and citizenship proof but faces Senate hurdles.
  • Senate has not proposed its version; action awaits a government funding deal.
  • Intra-party tensions arise over spending offsets and Planned Parenthood funding.

House Clears Budget Framework in Narrow Vote

House Republicans on Wednesday secured passage of a $95 billion budget framework on a razor-thin 216-214 vote, advancing President Donald Trump's priorities on defense spending for the Iran war, farm relief, and election integrity reforms through the budget reconciliation process.

Trump's Legislative Priority: The SAVE America Act
›Creates federal voter ID standard.
›Mandates proof of citizenship for voter registration.
›$10 billion allocated for state voter ID grants.
›Critics label it as voter suppression.
https://x.com/MarioNawfal/status/2079761772836192514

Three members of the Republican caucus broke ranks — Reps. Warren Davidson (R-OH) and Thomas Massie (R-KY), along with Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-CA), an independent who caucuses with the GOP — leaving Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) no margin for further defections.

"We're getting better at it every time we do it. Election integrity and support for our troops in conflict."

— Jodey Arrington (R-TX), House Budget Chairman

What's in the $95 Billion Package

The resolution directs spending across four House committees: $60 billion to Armed Services, $13 billion to Intelligence, $12 billion to Agriculture, and $10 billion to House Administration for election-related measures. The framework contains no spending offsets — a sticking point among fiscal conservatives wary of adding to the $39.5 trillion national debt.

The $73 billion defense and intelligence allocation is intended for the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Henrietta Treyz, co-founder of advisory firm Veda Partners, told Marketplace that "most of it is on munitions and operational costs for having our military deployed in the gulf region" — including military salaries.

The $12 billion for agriculture would support farmers facing what Treyz called a "double-whammy of the tariffs and also the war with Iran." American farmers are losing market share to competitors abroad because of tariffs while paying higher prices for fuel and fertilizer due to the war.

![President Donald Trump. Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg)

The SAVE America Act: Trump's Top Priority

Central to the package is President Trump's SAVE America Act, which he has called his No. 1 legislative priority. The bill would create a federal voter ID standard and mandate proof of citizenship for voter registration. It passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate, where it lacks the 60 votes needed under normal rules.

By folding elements of the act into a reconciliation bill, Republicans aim to clear the Senate with a simple majority. The $10 billion allocation would fund grants to incentivize states to adopt voter ID and citizenship verification measures. Romina Boccia, director of budget and entitlement policy at the Cato Institute, told Marketplace the money would likely go to states "verifying ID and citizenship before registering people to vote."

Democrats have condemned the provisions as voter suppression. "The American people know that this is a failed presidency, and this has been a failed Republican majority," said Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-PA), the Budget Committee's ranking Democrat, according to Reuters.

Intra-Party Tensions

The vote came after a week of intense lobbying. GOP hardliners raised concerns about the absence of spending offsets and the lack of provisions to defund Planned Parenthood. Trump intervened directly, posting on Truth Social: "I am asking all House Republicans to VOTE YES this week on the Budget Resolution... House Republicans must UNIFY, and fight for THE SAVE AMERICA ACT!"

"As a fiscal hawk I understand the apprehension of not having a clear payfor in sight, but as an American, I know it is even more irresponsible to have business as usual elections without the security the SAVE America Act will create."

— Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-IN), House Budget Committee member

Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO) had been among the skeptics, telling Fox News Digital that "the fact that there is no payfor and no language defunding Planned Parenthood is enough for me to vote no." A senior House GOP aide told Fox News that "Americans are tired of the all-hat, no-cattle approach to fiscal responsibility."

What Happens Next

The framework is a procedural first step — it directs committees to draft detailed legislation within their allocated budgets before combining them into a single sweeping bill. But the Senate path remains murky.

Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) has said the chamber will not take up the reconciliation package until a separate government funding deal is reached. The Senate Budget Committee also faces a leadership vacuum following the death of its chairman, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC).

Senate defense hawks want more Pentagon spending, deficit hawks want offsets, and some Republicans worry that pushing the SAVE Act could hurt GOP candidates in the November midterm elections, where polls show Democrats favored to win back the House. Whether key SAVE Act provisions survive the Senate's strict Byrd Rule — which limits reconciliation to items with a direct budgetary impact — remains an open question.

Senate's Uncertain Path Ahead
